text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The ruling Social Democrats and the Centre Party are close to reaching an agreement on a closure programme for Sweden's nuclear power stations that threatened the two parties informal alliance in parliament. Newspaper sources said the agreement would pave the way for closures to start sometime between 1998-2001.

- Sweden mourns the loss of Prince Bertil who will always be remembered. Many European royal families were represented at Monday's funeral to farewell the prince who died aged 84 at his Stockholm home nine days ago.

- Labour Minister Margareta Winberg and state secretary Peter Nygars visited the town of Arborg where Volvo Aero is closing down a facility to discuss ways to create more jobs with residents. The government is also in talks with Volvo about the proposed closure which would push unemployment in the town up to 15 percent.
- Prince Bertil, who died nine days ago aged 84, was buried at Haga park following a solemn procession through the city.

- Swedish exports are actually at a record high and not artificially inflated by companies through currency hedging or through incorrect currency exchange rates, an investigation by official statistics bureau Statistics Sweden shows.

- The government will be looking for Volvo to come up with some jobs to compensate for the loss of positions when it moves its Volvo Aero operations from the town of Arboga. Volvo has received a lot of state money in the past, Labour Minister Margareta Winberg says.

- In only a few years China has become telecommunications group AB LM Ericsson's largest market, almost as large as its U.S. market. Sales in 1996 are expected to total 11 billion crowns and have created 2,500 jobs in Sweden.
- Turbulence on the Tokyo bourse has hit Swedish insurance companies. Life and pension programme group SPP stock portfolio's value has fallen by around one billion crowns in recent months.

- Ake Hallman, the former head of nationwide Swedish drugs retailer, will have to pay back taxes and penalty fees on some 200,000 crowns he received in income for his duties as a board member of computer firm WM Data, tax authorities ruled.
